summary: A high basin on the borders of four prefectures, holding Ozegahara, one of Japan's largest mountain marshes, and the lake of Ozenuma beneath the volcano Hiuchigatake. Double boardwalks carry walkers across it from late May, when the skunk cabbage flowers, until the autumn colour of October. Campaigns here against dams and roads have made Oze a symbol of nature conservation in Japan; it became a national park of its own in 2007.

facts.suggestedTime: One to two days, with a night in a mountain lodge

story: Oze is a basin ringed by 2,000-metre peaks on the divide between the Pacific and the Sea of Japan. Eruptions of Hiuchigatake (燧ヶ岳), at 2,356 metres the highest mountain in Tōhoku, dammed a river and made the lake of Ozenuma (尾瀬沼), about 1,665 metres up. Below it, sediment filled the valley floor until Ozegahara (尾瀬ヶ原), at about 1,400 metres, became one of the largest mountain marshes in Japan. Its water leaves as the Tadami River over the 100-metre Sanjō Falls. Across the marsh, Mount Shibutsu (至仏山) is built of serpentinite, a rock few plants tolerate, and grows flowers found almost nowhere else.

The walking season is short and runs to a fixed order. Snow covers the basin from November to April, and in early May the boardwalks can still be buried. As it melts, skunk cabbage (水芭蕉 mizubashō) flowers across the wet ground from late May into June. Cotton grass whitens the marsh in July, daylilies colour it yellow in late July, and in September the marsh grass turns gold before the beech forests colour in early October. Japanese stoats hunt the margins and Asian black bears the woods. Sika deer have spread into Oze and eat the daylilies' buds, and the Ministry now runs a recovery plan against them.

From 1903 power companies planned to dam the basin for hydroelectricity, and their successor, Tokyo Electric Power, still owns much of it. The dams were never built. Ozegahara and Ozenuma became a Special Natural Monument in 1960, and in 1971 a road being built across the east of the basin was called off. No road crosses the park between Gunma and Fukushima to this day. In 1972 Oze began asking walkers to carry their rubbish home, and the next year removed more than 1,400 bins; in 1974 it became the first place in Japan to restrict private cars.

The boardwalks began in 1952 as logs laid over the mud. When walkers stepping aside on the single plank at Ayamedaira trampled that high marsh bare, double boardwalks spread across Oze from 1966, and replanting of the bare ground began the same year. The lodges have taken guests by reservation only since 1992. Ozegahara and Ozenuma were listed under the Ramsar Convention in 2005, and on 30 August 2007 Oze, until then part of Nikko National Park, was designated a national park in its own right, enlarged to take in Mount Aizu-Komagatake and the Tashiro and Taishaku mountains.
howItWorks: Oze National Park covers 37,222 hectares in four prefectures — Fukushima, Gunma, Niigata and Tochigi — and five municipalities, among them the villages of Hinoemata and Katashina at its two main gateways. Just over half is national land. Almost all the rest is private, most of it owned by TEPCO Renewable Power, the hydropower company of the Tokyo Electric Power group, which holds about 40 per cent of the park and about 70 per cent of its special protection zone. About twenty mountain lodges open in season, and the two visitor centres are run by the Oze Preservation Foundation.

Unusually, the park has no ordinary zone: every hectare is special zone, and a quarter of it, including Ozegahara, Ozenuma and the summit of Aizu-Komagatake, is special protection zone, the strictest grade. The marsh and lake are also a Special Natural Monument under the law on cultural properties, and a Ramsar site. In practice that means walking only on the boardwalks and marked trails and taking nothing away: picking plants and catching animals are against the law, and in the special protection zone so is collecting fallen leaves and branches.

Oze's own rules go further. There are no bins anywhere, so every scrap of rubbish goes home with you. Toilets ask for a small donation towards the cost of treating the waste. Lodges forbid soap and shampoo, because their treated waste water flows into Oze's rivers. Mats at each trailhead are for brushing seeds off boots, and walking poles need rubber caps. Private cars are barred from the road to Hatomachi Pass and from the road between Miike and Numayama Pass; shuttle buses and shared taxis run instead.

sights.name: Ozegahara
sights.note: 尾瀬ヶ原: one of Japan's largest mountain marshes, about 1,400 metres up between Shibutsu and Hiuchigatake, crossed by double boardwalks.

sights.name: Ozenuma
sights.note: 尾瀬沼: a lake about 1,665 metres up, dammed by Hiuchigatake's eruptions, with marshes and the visitor centre on its eastern shore.

sights.name: Mount Hiuchigatake
sights.note: 燧ヶ岳: at 2,356 metres the highest mountain in Tōhoku, a volcano last active in 1544. Climbed from Miike, Ozenuma or Miharashi.

sights.name: Mount Shibutsu
sights.note: 至仏山: a 2,228-metre peak of serpentinite with rare plants. Closed in the snowmelt season; the trail from Yamanohana is for ascent only.

sights.name: Sanjō Falls
sights.note: 三条の滝: the Tadami River, carrying all of Ozegahara's water, falls about 100 metres. A long walk from Miharashi or Miike.

sights.name: Ayamedaira
sights.note: A high marsh south of Ozegahara, trampled bare in the 1960s and being replanted since 1966. Quieter than the main marsh.

sights.name: Mount Aizu-Komagatake
sights.note: 会津駒ヶ岳: a 2,133-metre peak in the north of the park, its broad summit ridge dotted with pools. Added to the park in 2007.

sights.name: Ozenuma Visitor Center
sights.note: On the east shore of Ozenuma: exhibits, current trail and flower news, and daily guided nature walks in season.

sights.name: Oze Yamanohana Visitor Center
sights.note: At Yamanohana, the western edge of Ozegahara, about an hour's walk from Hatomachi Pass.

entrances: Hatomachi Pass (鳩待峠), Gunma — about an hour's walk from Ozegahara; shuttle bus or shared taxi from Tokura, as private cars are barred
Oshimizu (大清水), Gunma — about two hours on foot to Ozenuma
Numayama Pass (沼山峠), Fukushima — about an hour's walk to Ozenuma, by shuttle bus from Miike
Miike (御池), Fukushima — for Hiuchigatake and the trail to Sanjō Falls
Fujimi-shita (富士見下), Gunma, and Kozodaira (小沢平), on the road in from Niigata — quieter ways in
planYourVisit.reservations: Mountain lodges take guests by reservation only. Private cars are barred from the Hatomachi Pass road, so you park at Tokura and take the shuttle bus or shared taxi, and from the Miike–Numayama Pass road. The rules and shuttle dates can change from year to year: check before you go with the Oze Preservation Foundation.
camping: Three designated campgrounds, at Yamanohana, Miharashi and Ozenuma; camping anywhere else is prohibited
lodging: About twenty mountain lodges in the basin, open in season, by reservation only
Hot-spring inns at Tokura in Katashina (Gunma) and in Hinoemata (Fukushima), at the gateways
seasonalClosures: The roads to the trailheads close for the winter in early November; the walking season usually runs from mid-May to late October
Both visitor centres close at the end of October and reopen in spring
Mount Shibutsu is closed to climbers in the snowmelt season, roughly early May to late June — check the dates with the Oze Preservation Foundation before you go

weather: Oze's marshes lie between about 1,400 and 1,700 metres, in a climate of heavy winter snow, and its seasons run late. Snow covers the basin from November to April; in early May it still feels like winter, with boardwalks under snow and routes marked only by paint and ribbons on trees. The snow goes in mid- to late May. Summer days can be warm, but mornings and evenings are cold, so a warm jacket belongs in the pack even in July. Autumn is brief: the marsh turns gold in September, the beech forests colour in early October, and the first snow can fall at the end of the month.
directions: From Tokyo, take the Jōetsu Shinkansen to Jōmō-Kōgen, about 75 minutes, and a Kan-etsu Kōtsū bus to Tokura, about two hours, then the shuttle bus or shared taxi to Hatomachi Pass, or the bus to Oshimizu. Kan-etsu Kōtsū also runs direct buses from Tokyo. For the Fukushima side, Tōbu trains continue onto the Yagan Railway to Aizu-Kōgen-Ozeguchi, where Aizu Bus takes about two hours to Miike and Numayama Pass. By car, the Gunma trailheads are about 50 km from the Kan-etsu Expressway's Numata interchange by Routes 120 and 401, and Route 120 also links Nikkō over Konsei Pass. From Niigata, a bus from Urasa, a boat across the Okutadami reservoir and a reserved bus reach Kozodaira and Miike from June. No road crosses the park.

chronology.text: The first plan to dam Oze for hydroelectric power is made public.
Oze is included in Nikko National Park, designated on 4 December.
Ozegahara and Ozenuma are designated a Special Natural Monument.
Restoration of the trampled Ayamedaira marsh begins, and double boardwalks spread across Oze.
Construction of a road across the basin between Oshimizu and Numayama Pass is called off.
Walkers are asked to carry their rubbish home; within a year more than 1,400 bins are removed.
Oze becomes the first place in Japan to restrict private cars.
Ozegahara and Ozenuma are listed under the Ramsar Convention.
On 30 August Oze leaves Nikko National Park and is designated a national park of its own, with Aizu-Komagatake and the Tashiro and Taishaku mountains added.

safety: Asian black bears live throughout Oze. Be most alert at dawn and dusk, in fog, beside rivers and at the forest edge, and carry a bell.
Mornings and evenings are cold even in summer, and in early May the trails may still be under snow, marked only by paint and ribbons on trees. Carry warm layers, rain gear and a map.
Mount Shibutsu's serpentinite is slippery, especially when wet, which is one reason the east-face trail from Yamanohana may only be climbed, not descended.
There are no toilets on Mount Shibutsu or Hiuchigatake. Carry a portable toilet, sold at the trailhead shops.
regulations: Stay on the boardwalks and marked trails. Do not step onto the marsh, stand a tripod on it or sit with your boots on it; keep to the right, and give way to walkers going uphill.
There are no bins: carry out all rubbish, food scraps included, and do not throw coins into ponds or streams.
Plants and animals are protected by law; do not pick, catch or collect anything, including fallen branches.
Camp only at the Yamanohana, Miharashi and Ozenuma campgrounds, and light no campfires.
Brush your boots on the seed mats at the trailheads, and fit caps to walking-pole tips.
